source: Robs Pricing model / 'Pricing Model 6.0 Commercial Qu' (unit costs); Cheat Sheet (rates)
_notes: JSON has no comment syntax; this field is ignored by the deserializer and exists to keep the warnings next to the data they describe.
NEGATIVE COSTS ARE INTENTIONAL: flake_recovered and flake_recovered_double_broadcasted are credits for reclaimed flake. Nothing may assume unit_cost > 0.
QUARTZ: 1.0 lb/SF x $1.00/lb = $1.00/SF, the largest single material line on any double-broadcast job. Confirmed correct, not a typo.
SYSTEM RECIPES ARE UNCONFIRMED: membership was inferred by comparing four same-square-footage quote sheets. Every system carries confirmed:false until signed off.

CONSUMABLES are applied to every job but SCALED PER SYSTEM via systems[].consumable_multipliers. A multiplier of 0 means the system does not use that consumable at all. Seal reduces or omits most of them; applying them at full rate overcharges every sealer job.

CONSUMABLE MULTIPLIERS ARE EXHAUSTIVE: every system lists every consumable and there is NO default. validate() rejects a card with any system x consumable pair missing, so adding a product here without deciding its multiplier for all four systems fails to LOAD rather than silently mispricing. A default of 1.0 would silently overcharge sealer jobs and 0.0 would silently undercharge them; neither is safe, and a CI test does not help the person hand-editing this file. 1.0 = full rate, 0.0 = the system does not use it.
OMITTED PENDING CLARIFICATION: 'Whips' (source rate 5e-08/SF would need 20M SF to consume one unit).

GRIT ESCALATOR IS INERT: every grit_levels[].labor_multiplier is seeded at 1.0, so selecting any grit level changes no quote by a cent. The mechanism is wired end to end and waiting on data. Populate a level by editing its multiplier here -- no rebuild.

GRIT MULTIPLIERS ARE RELATIVE, NOT ABSOLUTE. What gets applied to an area is grit_levels[area grit].labor_multiplier / grit_levels[system standard_grit].labor_multiplier. A system's entered hours already describe work at its own standard_grit, so only the difference from that baseline may be charged; quoting a system at its standard is always exactly 1.0. Multipliers are therefore meaningful only against each other, and the scale they sit on is arbitrary.

GRIT ESCALATES HOURS, NOT COST. Labor, overhead, and the SF-per-man-hour readout are all functions of man-hours, so routing it through hours means every one of them picks the change up with no special-casing. More passes means more time, not a surcharge.

STANDARD GRITS AND THE LADDER ARE PLACEHOLDERS: seal at 100 and polish at 400 are reasonable guesses, not Jordan's confirmed practice, and the seven levels are a conventional ladder rather than the set he actually sells. Both are one-line edits. A system with no standard_grit (epoxy, polyurea) involves no grinding, and an area may not set a grit level on it -- that ERRORS rather than being ignored, so 'I picked 1200 and nothing happened' can never be a silent no-op.
RATES ARE EDITED HERE, NOT IN RUST. Changing a price requires no rebuild of engine-core or engine-web.

SCOPE OF WORK IS GENERATED, NOT TYPED. products[].scope_line is one customer-facing sentence per product and systems[].scope_intro / scope_outro bookend it with mobilisation, surface prep, and cleanup -- which belong to no product, so hanging them off one would make them vanish the day that product is suppressed. The narrative is built from the SAME resolved lines the price is: suppress the mender on a new slab and the joint-repair sentence goes with it, with no second list to keep in sync.

SCOPE_ORDER IS WORK SEQUENCE, not catalog order and not recipe order -- joints are repaired before the floor is sealed however the products happen to be listed. Sentences are deduplicated by TEXT, which is what collapses a two-part product (Mender Part A and Part B, flake thrown and recovered) into a single step: two catalog lines, one thing a crew does. Give two products the same sentence and they merge; that is the mechanism, not a coincidence.
